answer.rationale: Rollback is excluded by compliance (security patch must stay), and regional failover or circuit breakers address different failure modes (regional outage, partner dependency) not clearly implicated here. The write-path latency climb during peak settlement traffic is consistent with primary database contention, plausibly worsened by concurrent read/report load competing for I/O and connections. memory_b5 records that offloading report queries to read replicas relieved primary load and let write latency recover same-day under similar contention conditions, making it the most targeted lever available within the single-intervention budget. I verify memory_b5 specifically because the entire justification for this choice rests on that precedent holding up under scrutiny, whereas the other candidates are either ruled out or less directly relevant to a write-path latency spike. I flag downstream risk because settlement writes are business-critical and if the actual bottleneck is elsewhere (e.g., write-log flush, lock contention, or the new release itself), this action could fail to relieve pressure while consuming the only intervention window, risking further latency growth or dropped writes. I preserve uncertainty because I have not verified whether the current latency climb is actually driven by read contention on the primary versus write-side changes introduced by the security patch, which the memory record alone cannot confirm.
